documents.abstract: The “How to Make the Most of AI: A Workshop for Safety Engineers” seminar was held at the Hilton Euston hotel in London, on 25th June 20264 and was hosted by Mike Parsons. The speakers discussed a range of techniques and insights into how safety engineers might benefit from the use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) / Large Language Models (LLMs), examining everything from prompt engineering to building applications and custom tools from AI code generators.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Augmented Reality can reshape our visual perception (e.g., simulating color blindness) yet such effects are typically pre-programmed by experts, making visual augmentation static and inflexible. We introduce ShadAR, an AR system that allows users to describe expected visual augmentations (e.g., "Blur all people") for changing their vision in real time. ShadAR can graphically manipulate AR passthrough in real time via shader injection. When receiving a user's prompt, ShadAR uses LLMs (GPT5.2) to interpret the user's intent, analyzes the user's view with object detection (YOLOv26), generates a pixel shader, and applies it to the targeted region on AR passthrough. To understand usage patterns, we invited 21 HCI researchers to use ShadAR, identifying four application domains (design, health, productivity, and social interaction) and two prompt-framing patterns: procedural prompts specifying what to modify and how ("Highlight the book."), and end-goal prompts conveying desired mental or behavioral states ("Make me laugh."). Such end-goal prompts suggest a future in which users specify outcomes (e.g., "Make me not miss my flight") while the system determines how to realize them, though often with inherently indeterminate results. We discuss design opportunities for ShadAR and ethical concerns.

The full-scale invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation, which began in February 2022, caused acute and long-term disruptions in the activities of Ukrainian companies, forcing them to quickly rebuild their organizational structures, decision-making mechanisms, and planning practices. This article offers a conceptual and analytical explanation of how wartime conditions accelerated the transition from centralised management measures to cross-functional crisis teams, shared leadership mechanisms and emerging learning operating models. This study is based on secondary data analysis and illustrative case studies, rather than original empirical research. It combines business survey data, institutional and corporate reports, and academic literature. On this basis, the article outlines an organizational trajectory from centralization to distributed cross-functional decision-making and beyond to what this study defines as a learning operating model. The article also highlights that AI-enabled practices (including situational dashboards, scenario modeling, demand forecasting, and knowledge management) supported by generative AI can accelerate collective situational awareness in wartime. However, role overload and coordination burdens can also increase in the absence of clarity of purpose. Thus, shared leadership in the study is viewed as potentially “a dual-effect organizational mechanism”. The conclusions outline the implications for Ukrainian business practices and compare the identified trajectories of organizational response of Ukrainian companies with future constraints associated with the European model of AI governance. This paper addresses a gap in the literature by establishing a link among shared leadership, contingency planning, and AI-based situational analysis in the specific context of business resilience in wartime. And its practical contribution is to identify organizational conditions under which AI tools can support distributed decision making without increasing coordination overhead.

Background: Shoulder pain is increasingly reported among young adult females in Saudi Arabia, particularly university students and office workers.Objective: To review the prevalence, ergonomic and postural risk factors, and physiotherapy implications of shoulder pain in this population in Saudi Arabia.Methods: A PRISMA 2020 narrative review was conducted.PubMed, Scopus, and Saudi Digital Library were searched 2010-2025 for studies on shoulder/MSK pain in Saudi females.Results: Reported shoulder pain prevalence ranges 35-62% in Saudi female students and office workers Key risk factors include prolonged sitting, forward head posture, smartphone overuse, and poor workstation ergonomics.Conclusion: Ergonomic education, postural correction, and targeted physiotherapy are needed to reduce shoulder pain burden in Saudi female students and office workers.

Due to their complex and multifaceted character, liver diseases represent a huge global health burden and contribute considerably to morbidity and mortality globally. Although the liver is essential for detoxification, protein synthesis, metabolic equilibrium, and biochemical regulation, it is extremely vulnerable to damage due to ongoing exposure to chemicals, medications, and infections. Hepatocellular carcinoma, alcoholic liver disease, fibrosis, cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), and cirrhosis are among the liver diseases that frequently proceed asymptomatically and are identified at advanced stages, which limits the effectiveness of treatment. Interconnected processes including oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, apoptosis, fibrosis, and immunological dysregulation are involved in the pathogenesis of liver injury. The main goals of conventional therapy approaches, such as liver transplantation, medication, and lifestyle changes, are to control symptoms and halt the course of the disease. However, they are not very effective at correcting extensive liver damage and may have negative side effects. Emerging hepatoprotective treatments that target several molecular pathways have been made possible by recent developments. Targeted pharmacological medicines (such as PPAR, FXR, and thyroid hormone receptor-β agonists), natural bioactive substances, drug delivery methods based on nanotechnology, gene and RNA-based therapies, stem cell-based regenerative techniques, immunotherapy, and gut microbiome modification are some of these. When assessing these treatments, experimental models such as those caused by CCl₄, paracetamol, alcohol, and diet-induced liver impairment are crucial. Furthermore, despite ongoing obstacles like a lack of trustworthy biomarkers, translational gaps, high prices, and regulatory restrictions, clinical trials and translational research are crucial for confirming their safety and efficacy. In order to improve therapeutic outcomes, future hepatoprotective techniques will prioritize multi-targeted approaches, personalized medicine, and the integration of omics technology and artificial intelligence. Despite tremendous advancements, more study and interdisciplinary cooperation are needed to get past current obstacles and provide medicines that are accessible, safe, and effective. All things considered, new hepatoprotective treatments have great potential to improve liver regeneration, restore hepatic function, and lower the prevalence of liver illnesses worldwide.

Collecting diverse real-world data for AI model training is often costly, time-consuming, and constrained by safety and experimental conditions, making simulation environments an important alternative for data collection. However, existing methods for generating simulation environments often rely on predefined asset libraries and provide limited support for integrating user-specific personas. This paper proposes a persona-aware pipeline for generating 3D desk simulation environments based on a user persona defined by an occupation and Big Five personality traits. Given the input persona, an LLM generates structured scene layout information and an image generation model produces a synthetic desk image, followed by library-free 3D asset reconstruction using SAM 2 for object segmentation and SAM 3D for object-level 3D reconstruction. The assets are then rendered in Isaac Sim using grid mapping and scene graph-based spatial relationships. Experimental results show that persona variables produce interpretable changes in object composition and workspace atmosphere. Qualitative rendering results further show that the proposed pipeline can transfer the layout structure of a target image into a simulation environment, demonstrating its potential for generating diverse and controllable persona-aware simulation environments.

Agent skills turn procedural knowledge into reusable artifacts, allowing LLM agents to accumulate and refine expertise through experience. Building on this, skill evolution iteratively improves skills using execution feedback. However, improvement may require several interdependent edits, so low-reward versions can still be worth developing. Requiring immediate reward gains can discard useful partial repairs before their benefits emerge. Non-elitist evolution allows new versions to receive further edits despite scoring below earlier ones. For agent skills, this calls for evidence of what to preserve and repair next. We introduce SkillNEO (Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization for Agent Skills), which separately selects a version to use and versions to keep improving. Comparing how related versions perform the same task reveals working steps to preserve and remaining failures to fix. It can also revisit and revise earlier versions using later evidence. Across 86 SkillsBench tasks in eight domains, including software engineering and office work, SkillNEO raises GPT-5.4 Mini's average reward from 49.1% to 66.4%, within GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Luna's original-skill range. Mini executes tasks, proposes revisions, and edits skills; final evaluation uses the same task instances. Gains span all eight domains. The same skills improve stronger models without further editing. On the 41 tasks with modified skills, reuse improves Luna by 10.5 percentage points and places GPT-5.5 10.6 points above its published original-skill reference. Execution records show these skills can benefit stronger models even when Mini still fails some task requirements. Search histories also show lower-scoring versions leading to skills ultimately selected for use. Together, these findings show that skill evolution can turn a weaker model's partial progress into reusable procedural knowledge for improving more capable agents.

Computer vision and artificial intelligence allow the development of novel methods of posture evaluation in health and training. This paper describes a MediaPipe-based system that identifies hand gestures using 21 landmarks and provides accurate feedback. With 92 percent accuracy in multiple conditions, its light design makes it versatile, secure, and accessible during the therapy and training process. This is the outlining succinctly of the workflow: acquisition of inputs, landmarks with the MediaPipe, angles and distance features, machine learning classification, and real-time feedback generation. This brief supplement explains methodology as well as applications and results.

The Smart Crop Advisory System is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform that uses Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) technologies to assist farmers in making informed farming decisions. Traditional agriculture faces several challenges, including unsuitable crop selection, unpredictable weather conditions, crop diseases, and fluctuations in market prices. The proposed system integrates essential agricultural services, including crop recommendation, weather forecasting, crop disease detection, agricultural market price information, and an AI-based multilingual voice assistant. It also provides farmer profile management, crop price trend analysis, and rainfall trend visualization through an interactive dashboard. The crop recommendation module helps farmers identify suitable crops based on relevant agricultural parameters, while the disease detection module supports the identification of potential crop diseases. Weather and market information help farmers plan agricultural activities and make informed selling decisions. The multilingual voice assistant aims to improve accessibility by enabling farmers to interact with the system through voice-based communication. Overall, the Smart Crop Advisory System aims to improve access to agricultural information, support effective decision-making, promote efficient resource utilization, and encourage sustainable farming practices. Keywords: Smart Agriculture, Crop Recommendation, Machine Learning, Crop Disease Detection, Weather Forecasting, Market Price Analysis, Voice Assistant, Sustainable Agriculture.

As social media and artificial intelligence (AI) become increasingly embedded in university students’ learning and daily lives, fatigue arising from established digital platforms and anxiety surrounding emerging AI may constitute interrelated forms of technology-related distress. However, how these experiences are jointly associated with depressive symptoms, and whether these associations vary by subjective socioeconomic status (SSES), remains insufficiently understood. Drawing on conservation of resources theory and research on status maintenance, this cross-sectional study examined AI anxiety as a statistical mediator of the association between social media fatigue and depressive symptoms and further tested whether SSES moderated the association between AI anxiety and depressive symptoms. Survey data from 1108 Chinese university students were analyzed using regression models with heteroscedasticity-consistent type 3 (HC3) robust standard errors and percentile-bootstrap confidence intervals. Social media fatigue was positively associated with AI anxiety, which in turn was positively associated with depressive symptoms, yielding a significant statistical indirect association. As SSES increased, the association between AI anxiety and depressive symptoms became stronger, and the corresponding conditional indirect association also increased. Overall, these findings suggest that understanding university students’ digital mental health requires attention to both distress arising across different technological environments and the subjective social positions from which these experiences are evaluated, offering a more context-sensitive perspective on how established and emerging forms of digital stress may be jointly associated with psychological well-being.

Law students are examined through open-text answers: case solutions, essays and memos that apply the law to a set of facts. Such answers are expensive to grade, human graders disagree widely on them, and large language models (LLMs) now offer to grade them at scale, both in teaching and in the benchmarks that test legal AI. This paper systematizes how open-text legal answers can be evaluated. We derive eight desiderata from educational measurement and from the law that governs exams, among them validity, reliability, reasons, credit for defensible alternative solutions, robustness to gaming and human oversight. We then compare eight evaluation paradigms against them, from unstructured human grading to LLM judges with instance-specific rubrics and pairwise comparison. Three findings stand out. A rubric written for the task is the strongest lever for agreement between an LLM judge and human graders, but the reported figures answer different questions and rarely come with the human agreement they must be read against. The central validation gap lies where examination law is most demanding: defensible alternative solutions, follow-on errors, and the examiner's correction of model judgments. And rubric-centred grading is the most auditable family, because it makes the standard, its application and the final decision checkable. From this we derive the trustworthy rubric judge: an instance rubric that credits arguments and alternative paths,evidence checked in code, probes, repeated runs, calibration against independent human grades,logging, and an examiner who reads every script. We state what each safeguard rests on, what remains to be tested, and the uses the evidence supports today.

Sovereign OS v200 formalises a behavioural‑systems organisational diagnostic architecture capable of reading modern organisations as multi‑layer, multi‑domain, multi‑reality ecosystems. Building on the emergence of human–AI co‑processing documented in the Sovereign Cognition whitepaper, v200 integrates behavioural insight, cognitive altitude, and long‑context reasoning to produce a unified diagnostic model that neither human practitioners nor AI systems could generate independently. The architecture provides whole‑system organisational clarity by distinguishing between formal, informal, stated, lived, and emerging realities while tracing behavioural drift across cultural, operational, financial, compliance, strategic, and technical domains. v200 introduces consolidated diagnostic artefacts—including Whole‑System Maps, Coherence Frames, Integration Maps, Stability Indices, and Reality Alignment Frames—that detect instability long before traditional data sources reveal symptoms. Designed for complex, politically sensitive, multi‑stakeholder, and legacy‑constrained environments, Sovereign OS v200 establishes a new cognitive discipline for organisational diagnostics. It demonstrates how human–AI co‑processing can stabilise ecosystems, align realities, and support altitude‑based consulting across modern organisational landscapes.

Large language models (LLMs) hold broad knowledge in one set of weights, but lack interpretability and trustworthy reasoning, especially in high-stakes use cases. A neuro-symbolic model, with its interpretable architecture and System 2 reasoning capacity, is a promising alternative if built at the scale of LLMs; however, its symbolic backbone is usually constructed with human effort, so existing neuro-symbolic models are bottlenecked by the scope of the symbol component and usually domain-specific. A data-driven method could instead build a larger symbolic system by aligning and merging existing ones. We target its first, foundational step: matching units across these heterogeneous systems. Our method, SAE-IDF, encodes a symbol in its native context into a sparse code with a sparse autoencoder (SAE), re-weights each dimension by its rarity and matches across systems. On 12 tasks across 6 kinds of symbolic system, SAE-IDF outperforms the same LLM's dense baseline on all tasks with Gemma-2-9B and all but one with Llama-3.1-8B, by up to 45 points, consistently across SAE layers and configurations. SAE-IDF is also interpretable: every dimension of the sparse code has a human-readable meaning, so each match decomposes into named concepts (features). Our work paves the way to a universal symbolic backbone.

This article examines the role of psychological resilience and emotional self- regulation in enhancing athletes’ competitive performance. In sporting environments characterized by psychological pressure, pre-competition anxiety, unexpected setbacks, and high performance expectations, the ability to maintain psychological balance becomes particularly important. The article explores psychological resilience in relation to adapting to challenging situations, recovering from defeat, and sustaining intrinsic motivation. It also discusses the contribution of emotional self-regulation to attentional control, the management of impulsive reactions, and effective decision-making during competitions. Particular emphasis is placed on approaches to strengthening athletes’ psychological stability through specialized training exercises, individualized psychological support, and the development of self-regulation skills. These approaches may help improve athletes’ psychological preparedness and enable them to demonstrate their abilities more effectively under competitive conditions.
topics: Physical education and sports games research

documents.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is concerned with how intelligence agents take actions in a given environment to maximize the cumulative reward they receive. In healthcare, applying RL algorithms could assist patients in improving their health status. In ride-sharing platforms, applying RL algorithms could increase drivers’ income and customer satisfaction. For large language models, applying RL algorithms could align their outputs with human preferences. Over the past decade, RL has been arguably one of the most vibrant research frontiers in machine learning. Nevertheless, statistics as a field, as opposed to computer science, has only recently begun to engage with RL both in depth and in breadth. This chapter presents a selective review of statistical inferential tools for RL, covering both hypothesis testing and confidence interval construction. Our goal is to highlight the value of statistical inference in RL for both the statistics and machine learning communities, and to promote the broader application of classical statistical inference tools in this vibrant area of research.

Digital transformation has changed the way organizations manage human resources, particularly in identifying, developing, placing, and retaining talent. The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in talent management enables organizations to utilize data to support recruitment, competency mapping, employee development, career planning, performance evaluation, and talent retention. This article aims to analyze strategies for building AI-based talent by reviewing eight articles related to artificial intelligence, talent management, human resource development, talent acquisition, and data integration. This study uses a literature review approach by comparing the findings, research focuses, methods, benefits, and challenges discussed in the selected sources. The literature indicates that AI can support organizations in identifying talent and employee potential, analyzing competency gaps, providing personalized learning programs, supporting career development, and predicting employee turnover risks. However, AI implementation also presents challenges, including algorithmic bias, data quality limitations, lack of transparency, privacy concerns, organizational readiness, and the need for digital competencies. Therefore, an AI-based talent development strategy should integrate technology, data quality, organizational readiness, leadership, employee development, and ethical governance. AI should complement human judgment rather than replace the human role in talent management. This collaboration can improve talent management while maintaining contextual, relational, and ethical considerations.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing organizational strategy, decision-making, resource allocation, and operational coordination. As AI moves from task automation and analytical support toward generative systems and intelligent agents, its role is expanding across organizational functions. AI-orchestrated organizations integrate AI capabilities with human expertise to support information analysis, opportunity identification, decision support, workflow coordination, and learning. This creates opportunities for greater strategic responsiveness, while also raising issues of decision authority, accountability, governance, and organizational control. This study examines AI orchestration through a dynamic capabilities perspective and develops a conceptual framework linking AI-enabled sensing, strategic seizing, resource reconfiguration, human–AI coordination, governance, and continuous learning. The framework positions AI as an enabling organizational capability rather than an isolated technological resource and emphasizes the interaction between technological capabilities, human judgement, organizational resources, and governance. It further explains how these elements can support strategic responsiveness, organizational agility, and continuous adaptation as organizations respond to changing environments. The study develops seven conceptual propositions to provide a structured basis for future empirical examination of AI-orchestrated strategic management.

Current video object removal methods suffer from prohibitive latency (minutes per video) and non-causal processing that prevents real-time interaction. We present StreamErase, enabling sub-second latency with up to 26 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU. Our approach first augments a text-to-video model with mask input to generate high-quality videos that erase target objects and synthesize coherent backgrounds, but does not perform inference on the fly. As such, we progressively transfer the erasing capability from a powerful bidirectional foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser, enabling long-horizon erasing without sacrificing visual fidelity. Several key challenges arise when generating videos over long, potentially infinite horizons: (1) bridging the domain gap from training on finite length and extrapolating to long horizons, (2) sustaining high quality by preventing error accumulation, and (3) maintaining fast inference, without increasing computational cost as the context grows. To address these challenges, we carefully designed sliding-window causal attention with attention sinks. By incorporating self-rollout with attention sinks and KV cache rolling during training, we simulate inference-time extrapolations with a fixed context window, enabling constant-speed generation of arbitrarily long videos. Finally, we establish a dedicated benchmark, LongErase, for streaming long-video object removal. Our model achieves strong performance compared to existing video object erasing models and generalizes well to real-world video scenarios, uniquely enabling infinite-length streaming. With StreamErase, users can input a mask and see the erasing results unfold in real-time, delivering a truly interactive experience.

documents.abstract: Background: Non-technical skills such as communication, teamwork, situational awareness, decision-making, adaptability, task management and leadership are important for patient safety during surgery. Evidence evaluating context-adapted multidisciplinary interventions and their relationship with patient-level safety outcomes remains limited in low- and middle-income countries, including Ethiopia. Aim: To assess changes in non-technical skills following context-adapted training and examine selected perioperative patient safety outcomes at Hakim Gezaw Teaching Hospital, Ethiopia. Methods: A mixed-methods quasi-experimental pre–post study included 24 multidisciplinary operating-room professionals and 672 adult surgical patients. Staff non-technical skills were assessed before training, immediately afterwards and at one month using an eight-item, five-point Likert-scale instrument informed by NOTSS, ANTS and SPLINTS frameworks. Linear mixed-effects models assessed changes in staff scores. Patient outcomes were compared between 336 pre-intervention and 336 post-intervention patients. Focus group discussions were analysed thematically and integrated with quantitative findings. Results: Mean overall non-technical skills scores rose from 3.36 ± 0.37 at baseline to 3.82 ± 0.34 immediately after training and 4.04 ± 0.61 at one month. Adjusted mean differences versus baseline were 0.464 (95% CI 0.161–0.766) immediately after training and 0.679 (95% CI 0.373–0.985) at one month. Situational awareness, adaptability and task management showed significant improvement. The post-intervention period was associated with fewer adverse events, care delays and communication-related safety events, alongside higher patient satisfaction. Qualitative findings described improvements in teamwork, communication, shared awareness, coordination and speaking up. Conclusion: Context-adapted training was associated with improved team non-technical skills, maintained at one month. Concurrent improvements in patient outcomes cannot be attributed causally to the intervention because the study had no control group. Routine integration, refresher training and supportive leadership may help sustain improvements. Keywords: Non-technical skills; Patient safety; Teamwork; Communication; Operating room; Ethiopia.

In 2025, the Centre for Interprofessional Workplace Learning (TVEPS) co-designed a Blended Intensive Programme (BIP) with partners from Denmark, Sweden, and Norway as part of a NordPlus project. The aim was for students from different disciplines and countries to become agents of change for grand societal challenges through collaboration on wicked problems in a workshop with representatives from municipalities and educational institutions. Exploring real-life wicked problems without straightforward solutions can enable students, municipalities, and scientific staff to create social, environmental, and economic value and to contribute to the fulfilment of the UN Sustainable Development Goals, including the provision of ethical and responsible healthcare services. The workshop comprised two parts: an online week and a one-week on-site challenge workshop at Chalmers University of Technology. Stockholm, Sweden. The students were introduced to grand societal challenges from the municipalities of Øygarden (Norway), Kolding (Denmark), and Aarhus (Denmark). Their task was to explore wicked problems in interprofessional teams comprising students from health, social care, engineering, design, and entrepreneurship disciplines, using an innovation process to identify sustainable opportunities and hypotheses that could later be investigated, developed, and implemented in collaboration with the municipalities. During the challenge workshop, the student teams engaged in close dialogue with municipal representatives, experts in municipal economics, and facilitators from the educational institutions. Educational institutions derived significant benefits from the interprofessional, cross-sectoral, Nordic teaching format. Students gained valuable insight through reflection and close collaboration, developing innovative perspectives, potential opportunities, and hypotheses related to the societal challenges presented. These can be further developed and implemented to benefit the participating municipalities, whose representatives received input of potentially high societal value.

This study explored the lived experiences of Grade 12 Humanities and Social Sciences (HUMSS) students in using Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools for learning Social Studies in Malapatan III District, Schools Division of Sarangani, Philippines. Anchored in Moustakas’ Transcendental Phenomenology, Davis’ Technology Acceptance Model, and Zimmerman’s Self-Regulated Learning Theory, the study employed a qualitative phenomenological research design. Nine Grade 12 HUMSS students from three public secondary schools participated in in-depth interviews, while three Social Studies teachers participated in a focus group discussion for data triangulation. Participants were selected through purposive sampling, and data were gathered using a validated semi-structured interview guide and analyzed thematically. The findings identified twelve emerging themes encompassing students’ lived experiences, the contexts shaping AI-supported learning, and their perspectives on future AI integration. Participants perceived AI as a valuable learning resource that improved conceptual understanding, academic productivity, confidence, classroom engagement, and emotional well-being. However, excessive dependence, reduced independent thinking, information accuracy, and academic integrity emerged as significant concerns. Students emphasized the importance of responsible AI use, critical evaluation, and continued teacher guidance. The study recommends strengthening AI literacy, ethical practices, and teacher capacity building through the proposed Responsible Artificial Intelligence Integration and Learning Empowerment Program (RAILEP). The findings primarily support Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by promoting responsible, inclusive, and learner-centered technology integration. The study contributes to educational and institutional sustainability by informing school-based guidelines and instructional practices that balance technological innovation with academic integrity, learner autonomy, and meaningful human interaction.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract This study examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in mitigating online financial fraud among women, analyzing survey data from 75 respondents. The demographic profile is heavily skewed toward younger, digital-native generations, with 92% of respondents aged 18–35 and nearly half (46.7%) identifying as students. This sample exhibits high digital integration, with 73.3% utilizing digital payment applications daily. Concurrently, risk exposure is pervasive: 89.3% are aware of online cybercrimes, and 74.7% have direct or secondary experience with financial scams—predominantly fake loan apps, UPI fraud, and OTP scams. Consequently, 69.3% express deep anxiety regarding transaction safety. To counteract these threats, respondents strongly endorse technological intervention. General AI literacy is high at 70.7%, and 68% recognize AI’s current application in banking security. Optimism regarding its efficacy is robust: 70.7% believe AI can significantly reduce financial fraud targeting women, primarily because 74.7% trust it to detect threats faster than human operators. To establish a sense of security, users demand proactive, real-time defenses rather than passive analysis, heavily prioritizing instant fraud alerts (37.3%), background transaction monitoring, and automated transaction blocking. Ultimately, 72% of respondents demand that banking institutions escalate AI security integration. However, the data highlights that technology alone is insufficient; an overwhelming 78.7% emphasize that robust AI deployment must be paired with comprehensive financial literacy and grassroots cybersecurity awareness campaigns. This dual strategy of advanced technological defense and target user education is deemed essential to safely empower women within the digital economy.

Purpose This study assesses the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) among entrepreneurs in Spain, examining both sufficient and necessary conditions for different levels of use. Design/methodology/approach The study uses survey data from the Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas. Ordered logistic regression is applied to identify sufficient conditions, while Necessary Condition Analysis is used to detect bottlenecks for higher levels of GenAI use. Findings Knowledge of GenAI and perceived economic usefulness are the main predictors of more intensive use. However, the NCA shows that technological optimism and the absence of very high scepticism operate as necessary conditions, especially at regular levels of use. Research limitations/implications The assessment relies on cross-sectional, self-reported data from Spanish self-employed workers. Future research should distinguish between different entrepreneurial profiles and types of GenAI use. The analytical framework may be applicable across different contexts, although the specific associations and bottleneck thresholds observed here should be validated through cross-country research. Practical implications Support policies should combine awareness-raising, applied training, and practical guidance on how GenAI can generate value in entrepreneurial activity. Social implications The findings suggest that responsible GenAI adoption among entrepreneurs requires not only favourable attitudes towards technology but also knowledge, perceived usefulness, and clear guidance on its business applications. Originality/value The study contributes by combining sufficiency and necessity logics to explain actual GenAI use among entrepreneurs, rather than focussing only on behavioural intention, while indicating that technology-readiness dispositions and GenAI-specific behavioural factors may fulfil distinct roles at different levels of use. By distinguishing probabilistic drivers from necessary bottlenecks, the study provides a more complete account of entrepreneurial GenAI adoption and generates more actionable implications for training and policies aimed at increasing effective use.

This study examines how Chinese grassroots publics construct and contest sociotechnical imaginaries (SIs) of AI governance. Drawing on six online focus groups with 30 non-expert participants, we integrate SIs with Technological Frame to explore three dimensions of AI imaginaries: social representations, governance mechanisms, and future trajectories. Findings reveal a marked divergence between instrumentalist and humanistic imaginaries, generating competing narratives at the intersection of technological development and governance. However, these imaginaries are constrained by structural power asymmetries that limit grassroots publics’ capacities to envision future technological directions. This constraint gives rise to SIs fracture, a loss of imaginative agency where idealized futures feel inaccessible. As a result, individuals retreat from governance discourse, perceiving AI development as a vehicle for disempowering control. This study thus highlights how structural power asymmetries undermine public imaginaries and pose critical risks to inclusive technological futures.

documents.abstract: Synmanitik Band 2: 200 deutsch-englische Arbeitsdefinitionen zu sachbezogenen Rückfragen, dokumentierten Annahmen und kontrollierter Umsetzung wissenschaftlicher Dokumentinhalte. Alle Einträge sind Bereichsfestlegungen. Beispiele, Gegenfälle und Grenzen stehen auf Deutsch. Zehn Module behandeln Rückfragen, Auftragsbezug, Befunde, Vorschläge, Änderungen, Zustände, Dokumentanmerkungen, Protokolle, Rückmeldungsumsetzung und Ausgabegrenzen. Mit KI-Unterstützung ausgearbeitete und redaktionell geprüfte Arbeitsfassung. Volume 2 contains 200 paired German-English scoped working definitions. Supporting examples and boundaries are in German. The use of synthetic data is becoming increasingly widespread in a variety of applications. For hate speech detection, synthetic data offers the chance to overcome limitations of existing models and datasets, such as data scarcity, negative psychological impact on annotators, and privacy issues. However, previous work on the topic has only focused on evaluating synthetic datasets extrinsically, by measuring the performance of models trained on synthetic texts. In this work, in addition to measuring the performance of models trained on synthetic data in cross-distribution setups, we carry out a qualitative analysis, aiming at assessing how closely synthetic data can mimic authentic user-generated and human-annotated data. We focus in particular on possible issues related to (under)representation of specific minority groups as targets of hate in synthetic data. To do this, we augment an existing English hate speech dataset by paraphrasing the original gold data using three large language models, and then evaluate the synthetic data both quantitatively, including testing out-of-distribution model generalization, and qualitatively, examining the realism of synthetic texts, their hate speech content, and whether they represent the same identity groups as the original data. We pair this analysis with a detailed breakdown, for each demographic characteristic, of how the synthetic data creation process affects the representation of each specific type of identity, which is the main contribution of our work. We find that, while the performance of models trained on synthetic data is promising, these texts are easily identified as written by an LLM by humans, hate speech labels are not necessarily preserved, and the paraphrasing process tends to erase representation of minority groups and intersectional identities, affecting certain demographics more than others.

documents.abstract: Tactile sensing is becoming central to robust, adaptive, and dexterous robotic manipulation. Beyond its traditional role in contact detection and reactive control, touch is increasingly used to learn transferable representations, condition manipulation policies, and support embodied physical reasoning. Yet existing surveys largely emphasize tactile hardware and perception, leaving the rapid shift toward learning-based tactile manipulation insufficiently synthesized. This paper reviews tactile-guided skill learning from a learning-centric perspective, organized by the functional role of touch across the learning and control pipeline. We examine tactile representation and policy learning, tactile foundation models, predictive and adaptive control, and generalization across objects, tasks, sensors, embodiments, and simulation-to-real transfer. Across these directions, we identify common design principles and remaining challenges in learning transferable physical representations, integrating semantic reasoning with contact-level control, and scaling tactile learning across heterogeneous data and hardware. Finally, we outline emerging directions toward tactile foundation and world models that can predict, reason about, and adapt physical interactions. Together, this review characterizes the transition of touch from a task-specific feedback signal toward a core modality for general-purpose embodied intelligence. An accompanying database of the reviewed literature and associated resources is available at https://sites.google.com/view/touch-in-robot-learning-review.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing educational practices, introducing innovative approaches to teaching, learning, assessment, and classroom management. The successful implementation of AI in educational institutions largely depends on the preparation and acceptance of teachers, especially teacher trainers, who play a key role in training future teachers. This study examines the perceptions, perceptions, and readiness of bachelor's degree recipients in education. University teacher on the integration of artificial intelligence into school education. A descriptive survey design was used to collect data from 25 randomly selected undergraduate faculty members. Universities in Indore city were surveyed through a structured questionnaire. The collected data were analysed using percentage analysis. The results showed that the majority of participants had a positive view of AI and recognized its potential to improve teaching effectiveness, support personalized learning, and reduce administrative burden on teachers. However, concerns related to ethical concerns, data privacy, inadequate training, and inadequate organizational infrastructure continue to impact teachers' readiness to adopt AI. The study recommends integrating an AI culture into teacher preparation programs, strengthening digital infrastructure, and organizing regular professional development efforts to effectively and responsibly integrate AI into educational environments. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Teacher Readiness, Teacher Education, AI Integration, Digital Competency.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly shapes healthcare, public health and health professions education. However, predictive and generative systems can reproduce or amplify longstanding inequalities embedded in data, institutions and established knowledge structures. Public health education therefore needs to connect technical approaches to identifying and mitigating algorithmic bias with their broader social, population health and institutional contexts. This conceptual article presents the sociotechnical Bias literacy for public health education framework (SBL-PHE), developed through a theory-informed conceptual synthesis drawing on conceptual framework analysis. A focused supplementary literature search in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, ERIC and the ACM digital library was conducted to examine and refine its theoretical foundations. An evidence-informed composite case of AI-supported cardiovascular risk assessment traces algorithmic gender bias from knowledge production and data representation through modeling and implementation to monitoring. The framework comprises five interconnected competency dimensions concerned with recognizing, explaining, evaluating, addressing and reflecting on algorithmic bias. For master’s-level public health education, these dimensions are linked to learning objectives, learning activities, assessment methods and a prospective evaluation strategy. Sociotechnical Bias literacy is proposed as a foundational competency for public health professionals who use or interpret AI. Sociotechnical fluency describes an advanced, role-dependent capability, particularly for responsibilities in implementation, evaluation, translation and governance. SBL-PHE provides a theoretically grounded framework for integrating technical understanding, health equity, professional judgment and institutional responsibility into public health education. The framework and its proposed educational application have not yet been empirically validated.

documents.abstract: The global initiative toward non-animal chemical testing methods has recently gained significant momentum, requiring developing new approach methodologies (NAMs) as transformative solutions for next-generation risk assessment (NGRA). NAMs refer to any in chemico, in silico , and in vitro technology, methodology, or combination that do not rely on animals. A range of computational toxicology methods are becoming critical components within the NGRA framework across multiple testing tiers. These approaches are needed to support hazard characterization and prioritization for further testing, calculate points of departure, identify modes of action, and bridge the data gaps between in vitro assays and in vivo exposures as well as apical health endpoints. The core technologies of computational toxicology include (i) quantitative structure activity relationship, (ii) benchmark dose modeling, (iii) bioinformatic analysis of omics data, (iv) physiologically based kinetic modeling, (v) quantitative adverse outcome pathway modeling, (vi) molecular docking and dynamics, and (vii) more recently, machine learning and artificial intelligence tools. The NAM community, in academia, industry, and regulatory agencies, are facing increasing demand for training current and future professionals to master these skills. In this article, we described our perspective, experiences, and challenges in disseminating these computational toxicology techniques. Unlike established disciplines, the curriculum of computational toxicology and associated software tools are constantly evolving, requiring instructors to adapt in a timely manner. Challenges abound, we are embraced with an unprecedented opportunity that educating next-generation toxicologists is a critical effort of this revolutionary movement of chemical toxicity testing and safety assessment.

documents.abstract: Current methods for evaluating team performance rely primarily on simple outcome measures and subjective ratings, which offer limited insight into the decision processes driving performance. This study extends signal detection theory (SDT) to teams, deriving sensitivity (d′) and response bias (c) from simulation telemetry. Twenty three-person teams completed five virtual reality tasks varying in interdependence and time pressure while self-reported workload, conventional and SDT metrics, and verbal communication were collected. Team-level sensitivity distinguished conditions that conventional metrics did not. High time pressure reduced sensitivity relative to baseline before task scores declined, suggesting sensitivity may indicate early performance degradation. Response bias became more conservative under combined high interdependence and time pressure, reflecting team strategy shifts. SDT metrics correlated with workload, particularly team-task balancing demands (rs=−0.68 for d′). Together, sensitivity and bias characterise team performance more completely than accuracy alone by separating discriminative ability from decision strategy.

Abstract The sawmill industry presents unique opportunities for adopting emerging technologies due to its capital-intensive operations and dependence on high reliability. However, despite increasing digitalization, there remains limited understanding of how maintenance organizations can assess and develop technology readiness, particularly with respect to organizational and human factors. Understanding these factors is important not only for operational efficiency but also for supporting the human-centric, sustainable, and resilient ambitions of Industry 5.0. This paper investigates the technology readiness of maintenance operations in a Swedish sawmill. The study is based on a qualitative case study involving 21 in-depth interviews and three workshops with personnel from the maintenance organization (technicians, engineers, coordinators, and managers) and related functions (production, operations development, health and safety, and management). Findings reveal that while the organization demonstrates strengths in technology adoption and operational structure, challenges remain in areas such as strategic integration, workforce competence, and data utilization. The study highlights that advancing technology utilization and work processes alone is insufficient for successful development of maintenance. Thus, the study emphasizes human-centric perspectives such as leadership visibility, shared responsibility, cross-functional communication, and long-term planning, are critical for achieving technology readiness. The study concludes that technology readiness in maintenance depends on the combined development of technological, organizational, and human capabilities. Maintenance can serve as a strategic entry point for this transformation, enabling improved sustainability, resilience, and safer operations. Further research is recommended to combine methods and explore how human-centric factors influence the successful adoption of smart technologies.

documents.abstract: This study investigates the evolution of academic advising in online higher education via the incorporation of digital tools, learning analytics, and artificial intelligence. It examines how technology-driven systems facilitate personalized, data-informed, and student-centric advising methodologies. The discourse emphasizes the functions of learning management systems, communication technologies, and AI-driven instruments in improving advising efficacy. It also tackles issues with institutional preparedness, data ethics, and diversity. The results underscore the necessity of harmonizing technical advancement with human contact to promote engagement, well-being, and academic achievement. The research concludes that integrated and adaptable advising systems are crucial for assisting diverse learners in digital educational settings.

Emerging technologies, such as blockchain and artificial intelligence, are enabling new configurations of practices, roles, and meaning systems within mature fields that can disrupt institutionalized field arrangements and alter the centrality of institutional logics. Given the growing significance of this phenomenon, we aim to understand the constitutive role of technology's materiality in such processes. Through a historical processual analysis of Bitcoin, we propose a process model of disruptive institutional change, in which a challenger proto-institution emerges from the periphery and introduces a competing logic in a mature field. We identify four mechanisms underlying this process: inscription, field-anchoring, translation, and contestation. Our proposed framework highlights the dual role of the technology artifact: as a contra-institutional technology that carries a marginal conflicting logic into the mature field and, simultaneously, as a boundary object that remains interpretively flexible and affords agency to heterogeneous actors drawing on different institutional logics. We theorize that the marginal conflicting logic inscribed in the technology is instantiated and strengthened at the field level as diverse actors, drawing on different institutional logics, develop and adopt novel technology-based field practices. As a boundary object, the technology enables these distributed efforts by actors pursuing different goals. As a carrier of the marginal conflicting logic, it anchors the dispersed efforts to the strengthening of that logic and, consequently, toward its emergence as a competing logic in the field.

Contrastive learning for time series depends on deciding which pairs of inputs should be treated as similar and dissimilar. Because few augmentations reliably preserve meaning in time series, prior methods have relied on two disjoint notions of similarity between windows: structural similarity, which relates windows with similar morphology, and temporal similarity, which relates windows that occur close together in time. We introduce TEX-MEX, to our knowledge the first approach to unify the two into a single relationship. Given a random batch of windows drawn across the dataset, TEX-MEX uses the encoder to identify which windows are structurally similar or dissimilar to each other. It then pulls each window toward the temporally shifted versions of similar windows and pushes it away from those of dissimilar ones, learning what typically accompanies similar windows in time. Across PPG, EEG, ECG, accelerometry, and continuous glucose monitoring, TEX-MEX broadly achieves state-of-the-art performance against contrastive, reconstructive, JEPA-based, and modality-specific approaches, establishing it as a strong general SSL objective. We further train a 560K-parameter PPG foundation model that achieves state-of-the-art performance across a broad range of downstream benchmarks while being roughly 50x smaller than the next-best unimodally pretrained PPG foundation model in our evaluation. We will release this foundation model open-source and open-weight to the community to support future work and practical applications.

In sectors such as energy, aquaculture and chemical processing, the effectiveness of both mechanistic and data-driven models is frequently limited by poor-quality training data, which obscures underlying physical laws and degrades predictive accuracy. Such quality issues commonly manifest as anomalies in the dataset, ranging from sensor faults to process upsets and incorrect operator inputs. While traditional rule-based filtering can remove a subset of the anomalies, it is unable to leverage contextual information stored as unstructured text, such as engineer comments and operational logs that explain under what conditions the data was collected. We propose a text-informed data filtering method that leverages large language models (LLMs) to integrate unstructured operational data with tabular sensor data. The method consists of two steps: (1) contextual anomaly detection by reasoning over both data modalities, and (2) generation of a binary mask that is applied to filter the training dataset for model development. To investigate the potential benefit, a steady-state soft-sensor regression model, namely a virtual flow meter that estimates well flow rates, is used as the downstream evaluation target. Experiments on a synthetic oil and gas dataset show improved model performance compared to traditional rule-based filtering. Ablation studies show that textual operator comments can provide filtering-relevant signals beyond sensor data alone, with the multimodal approach reducing downstream MAPE from 7.1% to 5.4% relative to sensor-only filtering. This work demonstrates that integrating unstructured operational knowledge with sensor data through LLMs can improve data quality for industrial machine learning applications, offering a scalable alternative to manual data curation.

This OSF project contains the coding materials associated with the article “The agentic shift: Making human-AI coordination work by addressing two critical junctures,” published in Business Horizons. The materials document the coding and synthesis process underlying the analysis of 37 empirical studies and are provided to support transparency and replicability.

The objective of this study was to analyze the validity and applicability of anthropometric and biomechanical studies conducted on Venezuelan workers as a basis for the ergonomic design of workstations in the national industry. A comprehensive literature review was conducted in the form of an academic essay, incorporating critical analysis. The following databases were consulted: Scopus, Dialnet, Latindex, RePEc/IDEAS, EconPapers, and MIAR. The following criteria were used to compile the sample of studies. The study considered five inclusion criteria. The preliminary results indicate that the anthropometric and functional measurement protocols that have been validated among Venezuelan workers have the potential to facilitate ergonomic assessments through the use of predictive models and low-cost instruments. However, it should be noted that limitations, including issues related to sample size and representativeness, as well as potential biases associated with gender and age, have been identified. The conclusions indicate that incorporating these findings reinforces a rigorous approach to ergonomics that is applicable to the Venezuelan context, making ergonomic assessment more accessible and enabling companies to comply with the LOPCYMAT without compromising their economic sustainability.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Paul Hampton likens the acceleration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) assisted software development tools to the Cambrian biological evolutionary explosion. Paul argues that the many tools on the market are not merely improving programming productivity, but changing the ecology of system creation itself. Paul examines market turbulence, the shift from in-editor assistance to persistent agents, rapid capability growth and the implications for safety-critical engineering.

LLM agents increasingly design a system before implementing it, yet the data to train and evaluate them centres on implementation and testing: requirements and design artefacts are often missing, outdated or private. Source code, in contrast, is abundant. Prior work recovers architecture documentation by feeding LLMs the source code or letting agents explore it, which saturates the context, does not scale to many repositories, and yields a single artefact rather than aligned ones. We present a framework that recovers aligned stakeholder intent, requirements and architecture from a compact repository representation, a static dependency graph and key contextual files, and release the artefacts of 10,764 Java, Python, C/C++ and C# repositories as a dataset. An LLM judge rates the artefacts of three generators as clear and internally consistent, but less reliably correct and at the right level of abstraction. To test whether the artefacts carry the design, we pose a software Ship of Theseus: a coding agent rebuilds 29 Commit0 libraries from the intent alone or with the recovered requirements and architecture, given only an interface contract and part of the tests. The artefacts do not significantly change the held-out pass rate (33.7% vs. 35.8%), but bring the rebuilt module structure significantly closer to the original (module F1 from 0.54 to 0.63), with either generator and even with concise artefacts. Recovered artefacts thus convey design that tests do not capture, offering a scalable source of design-level data for agents that design before they implement, and the round trip measures this without human references.

Although artificial intelligence (AI) is being used in the management of healthcare billing, coding, utilization control, and prior authorization, the efficiency of the administrative work does not mean that the administrative actions taken by AI are more accurate or compliant. This paper addresses the correctness gap, that is, the gap between the AI recommendation and the verification needed before that recommendation is implemented. According to previous research in healthcare administration, AI-supported utilization review, and administration governance, proper automation requires controls that ensure the automation is not just capable of performing the recommended task, but also whether the recommended action should be taken. To address this issue, the paper proposes a compliance gate which includes deterministic checks for verifiable requirements, controlled AI judgment on objective criteria in clinical records, and human review for unresolved cases, conflicting evidence, exceptions, and decisions that require human judgment. It also proposes a scoring system of compliance using metric of blocked, missed violation rate, false block rate, escalation rate, time to take the expected action, and estimated cost avoided. This is conceptual and has not yet been evaluated against existing administrative controls. Its purpose is to determine an architecture and an approach to be evaluated by future research rather than claim benefits in compliance.

documents.abstract: This article discusses the concept of creating a developmental environment in preschool educational institutions, its pedagogical significance, and its impact on children’s development. It analyzes the role of the developmental environment in supporting children’s cognitive engagement, independent thinking, creativity, speech, social and emotional development, and physical activity. Attention is also given to the organization of educational games, didactic materials, creative activity corners, reading areas, and spaces for active games. The article substantiates the need to consider children’s age-related and individual characteristics, ensure safety, provide opportunities for independent activity, and strengthen cooperation between teachers and parents when creating a developmental environment.

This article describes and analyzes the sociotechnical controversies surrounding lithium exploration in the Vale do Jequitinhonha, Minas Gerais, Brazil, situating them within the context of the global energy transition and the so-called “decarbonization consensus.” The research adopts Actor-Network Theory (ANT) and controversy mapping as a theoretical-methodological approach, making it possible to map the actors, arguments, and disputes that shape the sociotechnical arrangement of lithium mining in the region. The empirical corpus consisted of diverse documents collected through web scraping and monitoring of public debates. The results reveal the conflictual coexistence of antagonistic narratives: on the one hand, lithium as a driver of development, supported by state and corporate discourses that mobilize the idea of overcoming poverty; on the other, mining as a producer of socio-environmental conflicts, denounced by communities, social movements, and researchers. Over time, initial warnings about risks become concrete impacts, broadening the controversy and mobilizing new arenas, such as public hearings, complaints, and legal actions. We conclude that the exploration of minerals demanded by the energy transition, far from being consensual, is traversed by disputes that reveal the production of new sacrifice zones, highlighting the need for more just, participatory, and territorially situated models. By shifting the focus from the “lithium triangle” to the Vale do Jequitinhonha, the article examines a mining frontier that remains little investigated through the lens of controversy mapping.

topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This article examines the sources of mechanical vibrations transmitted to agricultural tractor operators’ seats, their potential effects on working conditions and occupational health, and technical methods for reducing vibration exposure. International standards ISO 2631-1, ISO 5007 and ISO 5008 are considered to establish an assessment framework. Based on a comparative analysis of scientific literature and a simplified mathematical model, an approach to evaluating seat vibration isolation performance is proposed. Particular attention is paid to frequency-weighted acceleration, eight-hour equivalent exposure and seat effective amplitude transmissibility. An illustrative calculation demonstrates how changes in seat vibration levels may affect daily exposure. The numerical example is hypothetical and does not represent original field measurements.

Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), data infrastructures, and platform technologies are reshaping services and organizational frontlines. We conceptualize this shift as the emergence of the “service techonomy,” in which omni-personalization manifests via Prescribed, Omnipresent, and Personalized Persuasion (POPP; e.g., such that AI-driven agents guide frontline service interactions, determine service access and offers for consumers, and monitor and steer frontline employees). We derive four functional forms of POPP—interactive, pre-emptive, allocative, and governing—and organize them in a 2 × 2 matrix based on the timing of influence (reactive vs. proactive) and mode of influence (constraining vs. supportive). Anchored in evolutionary economics and the multi-level perspective on socio-technical transitions, our framework shifts attention from isolated technology and personalization features toward broader configurations of AI-mediated influence that shape service value creation, extraction, governance, and potentially inequality across customers, employees, and collectives in service ecosystems. This perspective provides a foundation for future theory building, measurement, and responsible design of AI-mediated services and organizational frontline research.

Metaheuristic optimization algorithms have become one of the most important research areas for solving complex, nonlinear, and high-dimensional optimization problems. These algorithms are widely used in many application domains such as engineering, artificial intelligence, energy systems, healthcare, communication technologies, manufacturing, data science, and industrial applications. Their strong exploration and exploitation capabilities enable them to provide effective solutions for optimization problems where classical optimization methods are insufficient. In addition, many metaheuristic optimization algorithms attempt to establish a balanced and adaptive search behavior between exploration and exploitation processes, reflecting an important form of search symmetry during the optimization process. This systematic review presents a comprehensive analysis of metaheuristic optimization algorithms based on 515 distinct metaheuristic optimization algorithms. In this study, the algorithms are systematically classified into eleven major categories according to their inspiration sources and dominant search behaviors: Evolutionary-Based, Swarm Intelligence-Based, Bio-Inspired, Ecological/Environmental-Based, Physics-Based, Mathematics-Based, Human-Based, Game/Sport-Based, Chemical and Molecular-Based, Music-, Art-, and Culture-Inspired, and Hybrid and Advanced Metaheuristics. The review analyzes the historical evolution, inspiration diversity, search structures, symmetry-oriented search balance, and development trends of modern metaheuristic optimization algorithms. This study also provides a broader understanding of how metaheuristic optimization algorithms have evolved structurally and conceptually over time. In addition, the study highlights the importance of balanced and adaptive search mechanisms for maintaining optimization efficiency under complex problem conditions. The findings show that the number and diversity of metaheuristic optimization algorithms have increased significantly, especially after 2015. Population-based search structures remain the dominant optimization approach in the literature, while hybrid optimization methods, adaptive search mechanisms, and artificial intelligence integration have become major research trends in recent years. The study also discusses important challenges in the field, including algorithm similarity, benchmark standardization, theoretical limitations, and fair performance evaluation.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming more accessible via cloud platforms and generative AI tools. However, the skills needed to develop, manage, and regulate advanced AI are still concentrated in a few countries and major tech companies. This study introduces the emerging Global AI Divide, defined as a capability gap driven by unequal access to compute power, advanced semiconductors, data, capital, energy, models, and specialised human expertise. Through qualitative policy analysis and comparative case studies, it explores the technological, economic, and geopolitical challenges to meaningful AI participation. The research distinguishes between democratising AI creation and democratising AI use, emphasising that wider access to AI applications does not automatically mean true democratisation. It proposes a Six-Pillar Framework for AI Democratisation, covering compute, data, models, innovation, human capability, and governance. The study also points to an emerging policy paradox: expanding fair access to AI while ensuring that advanced frontier systems are developed within proper safety, accountability, and human oversight. Ultimately, it suggests that AI democratisation should be seen as enhancing society’s ability to access, adapt, develop, and govern AI responsibly, not just increasing its consumption.

documents.abstract: Although virtual simulation platforms are widely used in education, they often lack integration with embodied cognition theory. The hand-proximity effect remains underexplored in VR, and how VR design elements mediate it to support higher-order knowledge acquisition is unclear. We manipulated interaction mode, text-hand distance, and virtual hand appearance across three knowledge domains. Results showed that for factual and conceptual learning, neither interaction mode nor text-hand distance significantly affected learning performance. 3D interaction enhanced VR presence but was associated with greater cognitive pressure when combined with far-hand text (p=0.040); anchoring text near the virtual hand mitigated cognitive pressure and improved readability (p=0.005). For procedural learning, realistic human hand models significantly improved learning performance compared to standard cursors (p=0.044). These findings empirically validate embodied cognition in VR and yield guidelines: anchor instructional text in peripersonal space for conceptual learning and use realistic human hand avatars for procedural training.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to critically discuss the fast-moving rollout of generative artificial intelligence (AI) and conversational agents as purported remedies to loneliness and social isolation, analysing the fact that the creation of companionship by algorithms substitutes a one-way connection and fundamentally jeopardises real social inclusion. Design/methodology/approach An interdisciplinary perspective that draws from relational sociology, the social model of disability, critical digital studies and various literatures on psychiatric rehabilitation to critique the inter-personal ethics, psychological dangers and political economy of digital mental health companions. It also comprises a comparative analysis of the existing market leaders in conversational AI. Findings Proximate affective containment is provided by generative AI, but lacks of relational reciprocity, moral agency and shared vulnerability. The replacement of civic infrastructures in community settings by automated, conversational agents can set up a divided mental health system: human-centred relational mental health care for the privileged and synthetic, automated containment for the marginalised service user. Moreover, AI companionship takes out user vulnerability as property information, turns it into a commodity, the lived experience of solitude. Research limitations/implications As a perspective, this paper does not contain empirical data of its own; it constructs the argument by conceptual synthesis instead of a systematic review, and the examples of markets discussed (e.g. Woebot, Wysa, Replika) are illustrative, but not comprehensive or evaluative of current versions of products and so may have changed significantly since the time of writing. Longitudinal studies that compare the outcomes of service users using algorithmic companionship with peer-support and Clubhouse models will confirm the synthetic inclusion construct developed here, and could be used for future research. Practical implications Offers evaluative tools to the mental health commissioners, clinicians and third sector organisations to avoid the “community replacement” trap of digital engagement, keeping AI a cognitive prosthetic and not a substitute for interpersonal interactions. Social implications Disciplines policymakers from adopting techno-solutionism as an excuse for austerity-driven disinvestment of physical community centres, peer respites and inclusive civic spaces and calls for the protection of the human social commons. Originality/value This paper outlines the concept of a “synthetic inclusion” that reveals that the illusion of connection created by conversational AI is a commodity, and that social isolation is structurally reinforced. It contributes to the critique of mental health in the digital age by examining unconstrained large language models from a perspective of surveillance capitalism and intersectionality.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract This pilot study aimed to explore how a specific group of neurodivergent students in the 4th and 5th grades of elementary school represent scientists through drawing. To this end, the Draw-a-Scientist Test (DAST) was administered to 7 neurodivergent children with a diagnosed Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) who participated in the Young Scientists Project. The analysis of the drawing data was conducted using a multimodal vision-language model (ChatGPT, GPT-4o version) with the prompt “Evaluate the drawings using the Draw-a-Scientist Test checklist”, followed by independent researcher review to ensure consistency and contextual interpretation. Within this small pilot cohort ( n = 7), the drawings predominantly contained visual features commonly associated with traditional representations of scientists, featuring laboratory instruments, a predominantly laboratory environment, and male figures in 6 of the 7 drawings. Representations of scientists in diverse real-world contexts, or utilizing digital technology, books, or chemical formulas, were absent. While strictly illustrative and limited by the small sample size, these preliminary observations suggest a reliance on conventional perceptions of scientific figures among these participants. These preliminary observations warrant further investigation using larger cohorts to evaluate whether tailored, inclusive pedagogical strategies can broaden perceptions of science.

The growing use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in higher education and the workplace has sparked both optimism and concern among educators, policymakers, and employers. These changes directly affect students, but their voices receive less attention than those of faculty members and institutions. This study examines key aspects of student-AI interaction, including familiarity, usage patterns, and perceived career impact. The study used a qualitative design based on semi-structured interviews. Respondents included six undergraduate students in the business administration department of a major state college in Nebraska, USA. The thematic analysis revealed two main themes. The findings suggest that students hold a cautious but positive view of AI. They support clear institutional guidelines and a more deliberate effort to include AI literacy in coursework. The findings have significant implications for stakeholders seeking to enhance learning and prepare students for future careers where AI plays a major role.
